recipe: atomicAdd blocks other invocations updating the same address. Two-phase it: accumulate into a workgroup-space array of atomic<u32>, workgroupBarrier(), then one atomicLoad plus a single store per bin into the storage buffer.

recipe: Storage pointers and bindings take access mode read or read_write, defaulting to read. Declare var<storage, read> unless you actually write. Do not write an access mode for other address spaces; they use their default.

recipe: Hoist conditional and computed types into named aliases and annotate return types explicitly. Named types are cached and compared by reference; inferred anonymous types get recomputed per use site and bloat declaration emit.

recipe: TS 4.5+ tail-recursion elimination applies only when the recursive reference is directly a branch of the conditional type (not wrapped, e.g. `[X, ...Recurse<T>]`). Such types recurse ~1000 levels vs the usual 100; use an accumulator type parameter to qualify.
source_name: microsoft/TypeScript PR #45711 (Tail recursion elimination on conditional types)
_original_recipe: Tail-recursion elimination applies only when a conditional type ends in another conditional type. General instantiation depth is capped at 100; tail-recursive forms loop 1000 times. Rewrite with an accumulator type parameter to qualify.
trigger_condition: A recursive conditional type hits 'Type instantiation is excessively deep and possibly infinite'.
_review_reason: 'ends in another conditional type' was unclear; the rule is the recursive call must sit directly in a branch; trigger was None

recipe: memo pays off only when a component re-renders often with identical props AND its render is slow. Useless when props are always-new objects or inline functions. No perceptible lag means no memo. Fix bugs, don't memoize them.
trigger_condition: Are props stable across frequent re-renders?

recipe: useMemo only for calculations that are noticeably slow with rarely-changing deps, or values feeding a memo'd child or another Hook's deps. Measure with console.time; roughly 1ms+ justifies it. Looping thousands of objects is the bar.
trigger_condition: Does the calculation take at least 1 millisecond?

recipe: useCallback helps only when the function is a prop to a memo'd component or a dependency of another Hook. Otherwise zero benefit. Blanket memoization costs readability, and one always-new value breaks memoization for the entire component.
trigger_condition: Is the callback passed to a memoized consumer?

recipe: Before reaching for memo: keep state local, never lift it higher than necessary, and let wrapper components accept JSX as children. When the wrapper updates its own state, React knows the children need no re-render.
trigger_condition: Are you considering using React.memo?

recipe: Keys must be stable and unique among siblings. Index breaks on insert, delete or reorder; key={Math.random()} recreates all DOM every render and destroys user input. key is never a prop, pass id separately.
trigger_condition: Does the code render multiple React siblings?

recipe: Anything computable from props/state is computed during render, never stored via useEffect+setState. To reset state when a prop changes, use key={id} instead of an Effect. For partial resets, derive from an id during render.
source_name: React docs - You Might Not Need an Effect
trigger_condition: Does useEffect+setState change state when a prop changes?

recipe: Code running because a component displayed belongs in an Effect; everything else belongs in the event handler. POSTs, notifications, parent onChange. Chained Effects that setState to trigger the next Effect are fragile, do it in one handler.
source_name: React docs - You Might Not Need an Effect
trigger_condition: Does the code run because a component is displayed?

recipe: Effect-based fetching needs a cleanup `ignore` flag (or AbortController) so stale responses can't overwrite newer ones. Prefer your framework's data fetching or a client cache; with no external system involved, you likely need no Effect.
source_name: React docs - You Might Not Need an Effect
trigger_condition: Does the code fetch from an external system using Effect?
_original_recipe: Effect fetches need a cleanup ignore flag or stale responses land out of order. Prefer framework fetching or useSyncExternalStore. If no external system is involved, you probably need no Effect at all.

recipe: startTransition marks updates non-urgent so urgent input stays responsive; isPending drives the spinner. The setState must be synchronous inside the callback, re-wrap after any await. Controlled text inputs cannot be deferred this way.

recipe: useDeferredValue shows stale content while the fresh render proceeds in the background: interruptible and device-adaptive, unlike blocking debounce/throttle. Pointless unless the consumer is memo'd, otherwise it re-renders every keystroke anyway.

recipe: Transitions stop Suspense fallbacks from replacing already-visible content, so spinners appear only for genuinely new content. A suspending background render under useDeferredValue keeps showing the old value rather than the fallback.

recipe: Subscribe to external/mutable stores with useSyncExternalStore, not Effects. React re-reads the snapshot before commit and restarts blocking to prevent tearing. getSnapshot must return cached/immutable data or it loops forever; hoist subscribe.

recipe: Async functions passed to startTransition are Actions: pending state, errors and optimistic updates handled automatically. useActionState for the common case, form action={fn} for forms, useFormStatus inside child buttons. useFormState is deprecated.
trigger_condition: Does the code pass async functions to startTransition?

recipe: useOptimistic renders the expected value immediately; its setter must run inside a transition or Action. It reverts automatically once the Action settles or throws, so never hand-roll rollback state.
trigger_condition: Does the code need automatic rollback after an async action?

recipe: use() reads promises and context and may be called conditionally or in loops. On the client never pass a promise created during render; use a cached one or one from a Server Component. Requires Suspense plus an error boundary.
trigger_condition: Does the client pass a promise created during render to use()?

recipe: Function components now take ref as an ordinary prop; forwardRef is slated for deprecation and removal. Ref callbacks may return a cleanup function, which replaces React calling the ref with null on unmount.
trigger_condition: Does the code use forwardRef for a function component?

recipe: Compiler is stable, auto-memoizing components and hooks on React 17/18/19. CONTESTED within official docs: memo page says you typically no longer need React.memo, compiler page warns removing existing memoization changes compilation output, so leave it or test carefully.

recipe: Compiler memoizes only components and hooks, never arbitrary functions, and memoization is not shared across components: the same expensive call in many components still reruns. useMemo/useCallback remain escape hatches for precise control.

recipe: 'use client' is a module-graph boundary: everything it imports ships to the client. Mark the interactive leaf, not the layout. Server Components passed as children/props are NOT pulled in, they render on the server. Render providers deep.

recipe: Sequential awaits inside one component are a waterfall. Start the fetches, then await Promise.all. Wrap ORM/db calls in React.cache to dedupe per request; identical fetch calls memoize automatically. Preload by calling the deduped fetcher without await.

recipe: loading.js wraps a whole segment in Suspense; a boundary placed next to the uncached read is finer-grained and preferred. Push async work deeper, await params/cookies inside the boundary, not at layout top, to maximize the prerendered static shell.

recipe: bitECS 0.4: components are plain objects of parallel arrays indexed by eid (Position.x[eid]). Prefer TypedArrays: zero GC, and required for SharedArrayBuffer multithreading. Storage is agnostic though; AoS object arrays are legal too.

recipe: bitECS recycles entity IDs immediately on removeEntity, so a stale eid silently aliases a live entity. Guard with createEntityIndex(withVersioning(bits)) splitting id and version bits (8-16 recommended), or mark-for-removal for deferred deletes.
trigger_condition: Does code retain eids across removeEntity calls?

recipe: bitECS v0.4 dropped defineComponent/Types, defineQuery, enterQuery/exitQuery. Now: plain-object stores, direct query(world,[Position,Velocity]), observe(world,onAdd(Position),cb). Full TS rewrite; v0.3 code does not run unmodified.
trigger_condition: Does existing code use bitECS v0.3?

recipe: bitECS removed Changed() in 0.4 as expensive diffing. Track mutation explicitly: observe(world, onSet(Component), cb) or route writes through setComponent. Don't rebuild automatic per-frame diffing; push the signal at the write site.
trigger_condition: Does the code use automatic per-frame diffing?

recipe: Structural edits during iteration corrupt query results. bitECS defers: query(world,[A],{commit:false}) or the isNested/noCommit modifier skips committing pending removals mid-loop; call commitRemovals(world) once at a frame-safe point to batch them.
trigger_condition: Does the loop remove entities while iterating a query?

recipe: Adding or removing a component is a structural change that invalidates live iterators. Flecs queues such operations during iteration (defer_begin/defer_end) and merges them at end of frame; annotate a query to force an earlier merge.
trigger_condition: Does the code change component membership during Flecs query iteration?

recipe: Archetype = the entity's full id list; each unique combination is one table of contiguous columns. Queries match tables, not entities, so iteration is column-linear, but every add/remove pays a table-to-table move. Batch structural changes.
trigger_condition: Do entities have multiple possible component combinations?

recipe: A tag is a component with no data, using the identical add/remove/query API and zero storage. Model boolean state as tag presence rather than a flag field; bitECS tags are just components with an empty store.

recipe: Row existence in a table is an implicit boolean. Don't store isRegenerating and branch per item; put only qualifying entities in the table so the comparison disappears. CPUs want the same kernel over contiguous homogeneous data.

recipe: Flecs runs one pipeline pass per frame across fixed phases: OnLoad, PostLoad, PreUpdate, OnUpdate, OnValidate, PostUpdate, PreStore, OnStore; within a phase, declaration order. Order at module level, never per-system: individual system dependencies are fragile.

recipe: Becsy derives order from query read/write entitlements (readers after writers) plus explicit before/after and beforeReadersOf/afterWritersOf directives. The partial order becomes an acyclic graph, linearized automatically with cycle detection. world.execute() runs each system once per frame.

recipe: Keep components small and atomic. A system needing only Position but loading a fat Transform drags unused bytes through cache lines. Split by access pattern, not by conceptual object identity.

Wildcard queries via ChildOf(Wildcard); Hierarchy(ChildOf) returns topological order. Prefabs use addPrefab plus IsA(Prefab) and are themselves excluded from queries.

recipe: Becsy stores fields in contiguous homogeneous buffers, not per-entity objects. Choose per component: sparse (eid-indexed, fastest, wasteful), packed (recommended default), compact (few instances). Set capacity when max count is known. object/weakObject fields forfeit multithreading.

recipe: Miniplex: entities are plain JS objects, components are properties holding anything (class instances, stores), identity is the object not a numeric id. Archetype queries via with()/without(). Ships no scheduler deliberately: systems are functions your existing loop calls.

recipe: In miniplex, mutate component values freely, but never add or delete component keys directly: that bypasses archetype reindexing and silently breaks queries. Use addComponent/removeComponent. Also hoist and reuse query objects; constructing one is comparatively heavyweight.

recipe: Contested: measured OOP-to-TypedArray speedups spanned 1.58x-24.9x, driven largely by spatial coherence rather than layout alone. The reliable win was GC: OOP p99 ran 2-3x its average, ECS p99 matched average. bitECS itself benchmarked 2x slower than hand-tuned SoA.

recipe: Contested, one benchmark: for CPU-only JS ECS data, Float64Array ran ~5% faster than Float32Array (5.32 vs 5.60 ms) because f32 reads convert to double. Use Float32Array when data feeds WebGPU or memory is the bottleneck.
trigger_condition: Does the code use Float32Array for numeric data?
_original_recipe: Contested: Float32Array ECS measured ~5% slower than Float64Array (5.60ms vs 5.32ms). JS numbers are always 64-bit doubles, so V8 converts on every f32 read, outweighing cache-density gains. Don't reflexively pick f32.
_review_reason: single benchmark (5% at one n); f32 is still required for GPU-bound data, so qualify

recipe: Archetype ECS in JS need not be purely SoA. Javelin benchmarked 5M entities: object-only 53.14ms, binary SoA 12.03ms, hybrid (TypedArray columns plus object columns for third-party libs like three.js) 25.97ms. SoA can't hold Maps/Sets.
source_name: Javelin - ECS in JS: Storage Mechanisms
